## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Claudinite work-item executor (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6, §10) — a pull worker
# over the queue. ONE RUN DRAINS THE QUEUE (§15.30, reversing §15.22's one-item
# run): Actions bills each job's minutes rounded up, so a run per item paid a
# whole invocation — checkout, setup, rounding — for each one. A run now settles
# its items one at a time until nothing is pickable, and the continuation job
# below covers a run that dies mid-drain. It carries NO cron of its own — the
# scheduler run's hourly dispatch, made when that run leaves something pickable,
# is the guaranteed delivery, so a lost `task:ready` label event is latency lost
# and never work lost.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the scheduler run and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A label event on anything else is not this workflow's business — and a
    # workflow_dispatch carries no label at all, so it always runs.
    # BOTH READY SPELLINGS, for as long as any fielded engine writes the legacy one
    # (#1119). A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing
    # here decodes — so this list is the one place the migration's two vocabularies
    # must both appear, and dropping the legacy spelling early makes every item an
    # older engine readies wait for the hourly scheduler run instead of starting now.
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # The old cap — ≤ the engine's executing leash — retired with the heartbeat
    # (§15.15). A run is bounded by a DRAIN's work now, and a holder that is alive
    # says so on its item every 15 minutes, so the leash reclaims silence rather
    # than length. What is left here is a backstop against a wedged runner, well
    # clear of any declared `code_work_timeout`; a drain the platform kills at it
    # hands its remainder to the continuation job like any other dead run.
    timeout-minutes: 350
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # The operator hold (DESIGN §8): set this repo variable to `true` and
          # every entry point exits at its first act, having fired nothing.
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
          # The wiring converge stamps every declared required_secret, and every
          # configured invocation endpoint's token, below this marker — by name.
          # claudinite:secrets
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  # A run that dies — crash, timeout, cancellation, runner loss — never reaches
  # its own re-dispatch, so without this the queue would sit until the next cron
  # fire. The platform runs this job on a FRESH runner after any such death
  # (DESIGN §10, S36), and its one step fires that dispatch instead: the
  # remainder drains in ~a minute, while the dead run's OWN item waits for the
  # executing leash to reclaim it — nothing here touches that item.
  #
  # `continuation_depth` is the stop. A run that dies at startup — a broken
  # engine, a revoked token — dies identically every time, and an unguarded
  # continuation would dispatch itself for as long as that lasts. After three the
  # chain stops and SAYS SO on the repo's workflow-failure issue: a queue that has
  # quietly stopped draining is the one failure nothing else here would surface,
  # since every individual run looks like an ordinary death.
  continue-the-chain:
    needs: execute
    if: failure() || cancelled()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const depth = Number('${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}' || 0) + 1;
            const ref = context.payload.repository?.default_branch
              ?? context.ref.replace('refs/heads/', '');
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${context.repo.owner}/${context.repo.repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            if (depth <= 3) {
              await github.rest.actions.createWorkflowDispatch({
                owner: context.repo.owner,
                repo: context.repo.repo,
                workflow_id: 'claudinite-executor.yml',
                ref,
                inputs: { continuation_depth: String(depth) },
              });
              core.info(`the executor run died — dispatched a fresh one on ${ref} (continuation ${depth} of 3)`);
              return;
            }
            // The chain has died three times running: this is not one bad runner,
            // and dispatching a fourth would spend the day proving it. Escalate to
            // the same one-open-issue surface the scheduler's own failures use, and
            // let the hourly scheduler run be what tries again.
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite executor chain failed repeatedly';
            // The platform reporting its own failure IS an origin (`task:origin:github`),
            // and a chain that has died three times is a break to diagnose — the
            // `failure` park, the one lane that holds a task's lane (#1119).
            const labels = ['workflow-failure', 'task:origin:github', 'task:status:needs-human-failure'];
            const ensure = [
              { name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' },
              { name: 'task:origin:github', color: 'd4c5f9', description: 'Claudinite queue: filed by the platform itself — a workflow reporting its own failure' },
              { name: 'task:status:needs-human-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite queue: parked — the run broke, diagnose and fix' },
            ];
            for (const l of ensure) await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, ...l }).catch(() => {});
            const body = `Three consecutive executor runs died before finishing their item. The chain stops here; the next hourly scheduler run will dispatch a fresh one.\n\nThe last run: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels, body });
            core.setFailed('the executor chain died three times in a row — escalated');

1	// Agent invocation (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §12, §14.6). The executor starts the
2	// agent session with an API CALL rather than by arming a label event, which is
3	// what retires the re-arm, the grace window and the transport dance — and what
4	// makes a lost hand-off a synchronous, visible failure at the executor instead of
5	// a label event fired into the void.
6	//
7	// A TASK NAMES AN ENDPOINT, NEVER A URL. The declaration is vendored verbatim
8	// into every consuming repo, so it must never carry deployment detail or anything
9	// adjacent to a credential: `invocation_endpoint: 'fleet'` names a key, and the
10	// repo's own config maps that key to a URL and to the NAME of the repo Actions
11	// secret holding its token. That indirection is also what replaces the whole
12	// self/fleet apparatus — reach is a property of which endpoint you call, so a
13	// task needing wider access names a different endpoint and nothing else in the
14	// system needs a concept of scope.
15	//
16	// THE PROMPT NAMES ONE ITEM AND CARRIES NO INSTRUCTIONS. Everything
17	// behavior-defining is read by the session from the tracked task files at HEAD;
18	// the prompt says which issue and which nonce, and the session validates both in
19	// code before acting (DESIGN §7).
20	
21	import { ENDPOINTS_KEY, LEGACY_ENDPOINTS_KEY } from '../../checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs';
22	
23	export const DEFAULT_ENDPOINT = 'default';
24	
25	// The endpoint is a ROUTINE'S API TRIGGER — `POST /v1/claude_code/routines/
26	// <trigger-id>/fire` with a per-routine bearer token — which is what Claude Code
27	// on the web actually exposes to an HTTP caller. Three consequences the design's
28	// "a CCR API call" did not spell out, each verified against the routines docs
29	// rather than assumed:
30	//
31	//  - THE BEHAVIOR IS THE ROUTINE'S STORED PROMPT, not ours. `text` reaches the
32	//    session wrapped in a `<routine-fire-payload>` block explicitly labelled
33	//    untrusted, and a routine acts on it only because its own saved prompt says
34	//    to. That is the issue-is-data posture arriving for free at one more hop: our
35	//    payload names an item, and every instruction comes from a stored artifact.
36	//    The routine's stored prompt is one line pointing at `instructions.md` beside
37	//    this file, so the whole of what a session does is tracked and reviewed.
38	//  - THE BODY CARRIES ONE FIELD. `text` is freeform and unparsed — structured
39	//    JSON would arrive as a literal string — so the item number and nonce go in
40	//    as prose, and nothing else goes in at all.
41	//  - THERE IS NO IDEMPOTENCY KEY (standing entry 11, answered: the endpoint
42	//    offers none), which is exactly why THIS MODULE CALLS ONCE PER ITEM AND NEVER
43	//    RETRIES. A retry is only safe when you know the first call did nothing, and
44	//    a client-side timeout is the one case where you cannot know — the session
45	//    may well have started. Retrying there is what would make invocation
46	//    at-least-once and put two sessions on one item; declining to retry is what
47	//    keeps it at-most-once and lets the whole agent-side claim protocol delete.
48	//    An outcome we did not learn is reported as UNKNOWN and resolved by the agent
49	//    leash, which is a rule that already exists, rather than by a guess here.
50	//
51	// The beta header is dated and the endpoint is a research preview whose two most
52	// recent header versions keep working, so it lives in config with a default here
53	// — a rotation is then a config edit on one repo, never an engine release the
54	// whole fleet waits for.
55	export const DEFAULT_HEADERS = Object.freeze({
56	  'anthropic-beta': 'experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01',
57	  'anthropic-version': '2023-06-01',
58	});
59	
60	// The endpoint a task's hand-off calls, resolved against the repo's config.
61	// Returns `{ name, url, tokenEnv, headers }` or `{ name, error }` — a task naming
62	// an endpoint the repo has not configured is a repo-configuration fact, reported
63	// where the operator reads it, never a crash.
64	export function resolveEndpoint(config, task) {
65	  const name = task?.decl?.invocation_endpoint ?? DEFAULT_ENDPOINT;
66	  // Either spelling: `endpoints` was renamed to say WHICH endpoints these are
67	  // (#1252), and a member writes its own settings, so the old key stays live until
68	  // that member's own converge rewrites it.
69	  const endpoints = config?.taskScheduler?.[ENDPOINTS_KEY] ?? config?.taskScheduler?.[LEGACY_ENDPOINTS_KEY] ?? {};
70	  const entry = endpoints[name];
71	  if (!entry) {
72	    return { name, error: `this repo's settings declare no invocation endpoint "${name}" (taskScheduler.${ENDPOINTS_KEY})` };
73	  }
74	  if (!entry.url) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no url` };
75	  if (!entry.tokenSecret) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no tokenSecret (the NAME of the repo Actions secret holding its token)` };
76	  return { name, url: entry.url, tokenEnv: entry.tokenSecret, headers: { ...DEFAULT_HEADERS, ...(entry.headers ?? {}) } };
77	}
78	
79	// The fire payload: which item, and the nonce that proves this call is the one
80	// the hand-off comment recorded. Prose, not JSON — the field is freeform and
81	// unparsed, so a structured payload would arrive as a literal string — and
82	// deliberately free of instructions, because the routine's stored prompt is what
83	// says how to act on it (see `instructions.md`). The session still validates
84	// the item in code before touching it: a payload labelled untrusted is trusted no
85	// more than a label event was.
86	export const firePayload = ({ repo, item, nonce }) =>
87	  `Claudinite work item: ${repo}#${item.number}. Invocation nonce: ${nonce}.`;
88	
89	// The invoker seam the executor calls, exactly once per item. Failure is DATA,
90	// never a throw, and it comes in two kinds the caller must treat differently:
91	//
92	//   { ok: true, sessionId, sessionUrl }   the routine fired; a session exists
93	//   { ok: false, answered: true, error }  the endpoint ANSWERED and refused —
94	//                                         no session, and the cause is a
95	//                                         configuration fault a retry cannot fix
96	//   { ok: false, answered: false, error } no answer reached us — a timeout, a
97	//                                         dropped connection. The session may or
98	//                                         may not exist, and nothing here may
99	//                                         guess which.
100	export function agentInvoker({ repo, config, env = process.env, fetchImpl = fetch, timeoutMs = 60e3 }) {
101	  return async function invoke({ task, item, nonce }) {
102	    const endpoint = resolveEndpoint(config, task);
103	    // A configuration fault, decided before any call: definite, and no session.
104	    if (endpoint.error) return { ok: false, answered: true, error: endpoint.error };
105	    const token = env[endpoint.tokenEnv];
106	    if (!token) {
107	      // The `required_secrets` posture, applied to the endpoint token: nothing
108	      // fails silently, the task just doesn't work yet, and the item names which
109	      // secret to set (DESIGN §14.7).
110	      return { ok: false, answered: true, error: `the Actions secret \`${endpoint.tokenEnv}\` for invocation endpoint "${endpoint.name}" is not set in this repo` };
111	    }
112	
113	    const payload = { text: firePayload({ repo, item, nonce }) };
114	
115	    // ONE call. No loop, and deliberately no `attempts` knob for anyone to raise.
116	    try {
117	      const res = await fetchImpl(endpoint.url, {
118	        method: 'POST',
119	        headers: {
120	          ...endpoint.headers,
121	          'content-type': 'application/json',
122	          authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
123	          'user-agent': 'claudinite-executor',
124	        },
125	        body: JSON.stringify(payload),
126	        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
127	      });
128	      let json = null;
129	      try { json = await res.json(); } catch { json = null; }
130	      if (res.status >= 200 && res.status < 300) {
131	        return {
132	          ok: true,
133	          sessionId: json?.claude_code_session_id ?? null,
134	          sessionUrl: json?.claude_code_session_url ?? null,
135	        };
136	      }
137	      // A status came back, so the endpoint decided: no session was started, and
138	      // the cause is a token, a URL or a routine — none of which a retry fixes.
139	      return {
140	        ok: false, answered: true,
141	        error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" returned ${res.status}${json?.error ? `: ${JSON.stringify(json.error)}` : ''}`,
142	      };
143	    } catch (e) {
144	      // Nothing came back. The request may have landed and started a session, so
145	      // this is the one outcome that must never be retried and never be reported
146	      // as a failure — it is genuinely unknown, and the caller says so on the item.
147	      return { ok: false, answered: false, error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" gave no answer: ${e.message}` };
148	    }
149	  };
150	}

# Claude Code agent proxy

Outbound HTTPS from this session goes through a local proxy at [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]
(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
[REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Run: curl -sS [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]/__agentproxy/status
   It reports proxy state, which trust and git accommodations are active
   (javaTrustStorePath, toolTrustFailureCodes, gitSshRewrite,
   gitConfigConflicts), and the most recent proxy-side failures.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix; gitConfigConflicts
   codes map to the git section, toolTrustFailureCodes to the JVM section.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   organization policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at [REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present, a truststore
  is built at /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit") and
  injected via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS — confirm javaTrustStorePath is set in the
  status output before pointing a build at it (toolTrustFailureCodes explains
  why it is missing). If the image or the build sets its own trustStore, that
